Empirical Research Plan  

================================================================  
1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Main goal: measure how exogenous land scarcity conditions the price-vs-quantity response of metropolitan housing markets to demand shocks and how the political choice of land-use regulation feeds back into that mechanism.

Methodological core = Difference-in-Differences with continuous treatment (a.k.a. an interacted event‐study / triple-difference), supplemented with an IV for regulatory stringency.

•  Cross-section dimension: permanent, exogenous physical‐land constraint of MSA i (Slope>15 %, water, wetlands, coastline share).  
•  Time dimension: plausibly exogenous, national demand shocks that strike all metros but with different intensity – we will use a Bartik-style predicted immigration shock and a predicted industrial-composition shock.  
•  Identification: compare the change in ln-housing prices (or ln-housing units) between 1970–2000 in high-constraint versus low-constraint metros while both are hit by the same national demand shock. Formally, estimate the interaction of constraint_i with time-varying shock_it, controlling for MSA and year FEs.  β answers: “When demand rises by 1 pp, how much more does price grow (and how much less do quantities grow) in a highly constrained metro relative to a flat, dry metro?”  

To study local regulation we treat the 2005 Wharton index as an endogenous policy outcome and use 2SLS: first stage instruments regulation_i with the vector of natural constraints interacted with historical homeowner share and county-level fiscal‐conservatism proxies (plausibly exogenous to the 2000–05 housing boom once metropolitan fixed effects are partialed out).

Hence two complementary strategies:  
(1) DiD / Triple-Diff for physical constraints × demand shocks.  
(2) Cross-section IV for regulatory stringency conditional on constraints.

================================================================  
2. Treatment and Control  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Physical-constraint experiment (main specification)  
•  Treatment variable: Constr_i = share of land within 50 km that is undevelopable (slope>15 %, water, wetlands, ocean-coast lost area). Continuous 0–1; we normalise to mean 0, sd 1.  
•  Time-varying “shock”: Shock_it = predicted demand growth for MSA i in decade t. Baseline = immigration Bartik: Σ_origin (NationalImm_growth_ot × base share_io,1970). Alternative shock = industry-Bartik (national employment growth in each 2-digit industry × 1970 industry shares).  
•  Counterfactual: low-constraint MSAs provide untreated potential outcome; Shock_it varies for both groups.  
•  Timing / event: each decennial interval (1970-80, 80-90, 90-00).  

Regulation experiment (auxiliary):  
•  Endogenous regressor: Reg_i = 2005 Wharton index (higher = stricter).  
•  Instruments: (i) Constr_i – physical scarcity raises homeowner incentives to protect rents, (ii) Constr_i × 1970 homeowner rate, (iii) log(distance to nearest coastline) interacted with county GOP vote share 1968-72 (captures taste for regulation unrelated to 2000s price boom).  
•  Control group: metros predicted to have low regulation by the first stage.

================================================================  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1.  Parallel trends: absent the demand shock, price and quantity trajectories in high- and low-constraint MSAs would have followed parallel paths.  
Plausibility: physical geography is time-invariant and was largely priced-in prior to 1970; long‐run demographic evolutions unrelated to geography are absorbed by MSA FEs and decade FEs.

A2.  Exogeneity of Bartik shocks: national immigration composition (or national industry growth) is orthogonal to local housing-supply conditions conditional on baseline shares. Literature supports this, and we control for differential long-run industry/ethnic trends.

A3.  Stable constraint measure: land converted from undevelopable to developable (e.g., landfill, mountain blasting) is negligible over 1970-2000.

A4.  For IV: exclusion – physical constraints influence current prices only through regulation once we directly control for interaction of constraints with demand shocks (i.e., the direct supply-elasticity channel). We include Constr_i × Shock_it terms in the second stage to soak up the direct effect.

================================================================  
4. Threats to Identification and Remedies  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
T1.  Endogenous migration: workers may choose constrained metros because of amenities or labour demand, biasing β upward.  
Remedy: use only predicted immigration shocks (shift-share) that rely on nationwide origin growth, not realised local inflows; control for time-varying amenities (sun-hours, tourist visits, etc.).  

T2.  Omitted policy co-movements (e.g., transport spending, tax changes) correlated with constraints.  
Remedy: include controls for per-capita highway spending, local public service expenditures, and MSA-specific linear trends; run placebo on non-housing outcomes (e.g., grocery CPI) to show no differential trend.  

T3.  Weak first-stage for regulation IV.  
Remedy: report Kleibergen-Paap F-stat; collapse instruments to strongest interaction; if weak, present LIML estimates and a Conley et al. (2012) bias-correction.

================================================================  
5. R Code Outline  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# --- 0. Packages -----------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # TWFE regressions
library(ivreg)        # 2SLS
library(modelsummary) # nice tables

# --- 1. Load Data ----------------------------------------------------------
panel  <- fread("msa_panel_1970_2000.csv")      # yearly or decennial data
cross  <- fread("msa_crosssection.csv")         # 2005 Wharton etc.

# --- 2. Variable Construction ---------------------------------------------
# Physical constraint (standardised)
panel[, constr := (slope_share + water_share + wetland_share)/100 ]
panel[, constr_z := scale(constr)]

# Bartik immigration shock
# nat_imm_growth_ot  already in panel at decade t by origin
panel[, imm_bartik := rowSums(.SD), by = .(msa, decade),
      .SDcols = patterns("^imm_growth_")]   # sum over origins * 1970 shares

# Outcomes
panel[, dln_price  := log(hpi) - shift(log(hpi)), by = msa]
panel[, dln_units  := log(housing_units) - shift(log(housing_units)), by = msa]

# --- 3. Main DiD Specification --------------------------------------------
# Prices
did_price <- feols(dln_price ~ constr_z*imm_bartik + imm_bartik + constr_z |
                   msa + decade, cluster = ~msa, data = panel)
# Quantities
did_units <- feols(dln_units ~ constr_z*imm_bartik + imm_bartik + constr_z |
                   msa + decade, cluster = ~msa, data = panel)

# --- 4. IV for Regulation --------------------------------------------------
cross[, reg_z := scale(wharton_index)]
cross[, homeowner70 := homeowner_share_1970]

# Instruments
cross[, z1 := constr_z]
cross[, z2 := constr_z * homeowner70]
cross[, z3 := constr_z * gop681972]

iv_formula <- reg_z ~ constr_z + homeowner70 | z1 + z2 + z3 + homeowner70

reg_iv <- ivreg(iv_formula, data = cross)

# Second stage: effect of regulation on price elasticity to demand
# merge first-stage fitted values back to panel
panel <- merge(panel, cross[, .(msa, reg_hat = fitted(reg_iv))], by = "msa")

did_price_reg <- feols(dln_price ~ reg_hat*imm_bartik + constr_z*imm_bartik +
                       imm_bartik + reg_hat + constr_z |
                       msa + decade, cluster = ~msa, data = panel)

# --- 5. Robustness: MSA-specific time trends ------------------------------
panel[, trend := decade - 1970]
did_price_tr <- feols(dln_price ~ constr_z*imm_bartik + imm_bartik + constr_z |
                      msa + decade + msa[trend], cluster = ~msa, data = panel)

# --- 6. Output -------------------------------------------------------------
modelsummary(list(Main = did_price, TrendRobust = did_price_tr),
             gof_omit = "IC|Adj|F")
```

================================================================  
6. Expected Results  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
•  β_Price > 0: a one-sd higher land-constraint metro should translate a 1 pp immigration shock into roughly 1.2–1.5 pp extra price growth per decade.  
•  β_Quantity < 0: same metro should build about 0.5 pp fewer housing units per 1 pp demand shock.  
•  Regulation: one-sd rise in the Wharton index likely magnifies the price response by 0.4 pp and attenuates quantity response by similar magnitude.

================================================================  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: Pre-trend balance graphs / event study show no differential trends – 0.8  
C2: No simultaneous shocks correlated with both constraint and outcomes – 0.6  
C3: Correct functional form / no heterogeneous treatment timing bias – 0.8  
C4: No compositional change in MSA definitions – 0.9  
C5: SUTVA (no spillovers across MSAs) – 0.7  

Average ≈ 0.76 ⇒ reasonably credible but not bullet-proof.

================================================================
